#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Dataset integrity + schema check. Usage: python3 scripts/verify.py [--rebuild]"""
import hashlib, json, os, sys

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
DATA = os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "entries.dat")
DIGEST = os.path.join(ROOT, "data", ".digest")

digest = hashlib.sha256(open(DATA, "rb").read()).hexdigest()
if "--rebuild" in sys.argv:
    open(DIGEST, "w").write(digest)
    print("digest rebuilt")
    sys.exit(0)
if not os.path.exists(DIGEST) or open(DIGEST).read().strip() != digest:
    sys.exit("FAIL: digest mismatch (data/.digest does not match data/entries.dat)")
n = 0
for i, line in enumerate(open(DATA, encoding="utf-8"), 1):
    if not line.strip():
        continue
    try:
        e = json.loads(line)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        sys.exit("FAIL: line %d is not valid JSON" % i)
    if sorted(e) != ["prompt", "response"]:
        sys.exit("FAIL: line %d has wrong schema" % i)
    n += 1
print("ALL CHECKS PASSED (%d entries)" % n)

final_entries.prompt: My Go program panics with 'slice bounds out of range' but only when processing a large input file.
final_entries.response: This is a classic off-by-one or empty-slice issue that manifests under certain data conditions. Check every slice operation — especially `arr[start:end]` where `end` could equal `len(arr)+1`, or `arr[:n]` when the slice is empty (n=0 on empty slice is fine, but `arr[-1:]` on empty slice panics). Also watch for concurrent modifications: if one goroutine is shrinking a slice while another reads it, the bounds can shift. The easiest fix is to add `if len(s) == 0 { return }` guards before every slice, or use `min/end` bounds: `arr[start:min(end, len(arr))]`. Run with `go run -gcflags="-l"` to disable inlining for cleaner stack traces.

final_entries.prompt: My Rust program won't compile and gives a borrows error about a mutable borrow conflicting with an immutable one, but I'm not holding any references explicitly.
final_entries.response: Rust's borrow checker is catching a hidden reference you might not see. The most common culprit: calling `.iter()` or `.as_slice()` on a collection and then trying to mutate that same collection in the same scope. Even if the iterator variable is "done" by the time you mutate, Rust's borrow rules are static, not dynamic — the borrow lasts for its entire lexical scope. Fix options: (1) use a `let _scope = { ... };` block to limit the borrow's lifetime, (2) collect the iterator into a `Vec` first (`.collect::<Vec<_>>()`), or (3) restructure so the mutable operation happens in a separate scope. If you're using `for x in &mut collection`, check if anything inside the loop body needs the whole collection by immutable reference — that's your conflict.

final_entries.prompt: After upgrading to Node 18, my Express app crashes on startup with "ERR_REQUIRE_ESM" — nothing worked before the upgrade.
final_entries.response: This happens when a package your project depends on switched to ESM-only distribution (dropping CommonJS support) in a newer version. The upgrade may have pulled in a newer dependency transitively. First, check which package is the culprit: look at the full error stack — it usually names the file. Then either: (1) add `"type": "module"` to your package.json and convert your app to ESM (use `import` instead of `require`, use `import.meta.url` instead of `__dirname`), or (2) pin the problematic dependency to its last CommonJS-compatible version in your lock file. A quick diagnostic: run `npm ls <suspect-package>` to see which version resolved, then check its package.json on npm for `"type": "module"`. If you're stuck, you can also use `createRequire` from Node's `module` package as a bridge: `const { createRequire } = require(module); const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);`.

final_entries.prompt: My Flask app works locally but returns a 413 Request Entity Too Large on our production server. I'm uploading files under 1 MB.
final_entries.response: The 413 error comes from your web server or reverse proxy, not Flask itself. The most common culprits: Nginx has `client_max_body_size` (defaults to 1MB) in its config — add `client_max_body_size 10M;` in your server block. Apache has `LimitRequestBody` (defaults to unlimited, but some distros change it) — set `LimitRequestBody 10485760` (10MB in bytes). If you're behind CloudFront or Cloudflare, check their limits too (CloudFront defaults to 100MB but can be configured lower). Also double-check that you're not hitting the limit in bytes — a 1MB file in base64 encoding is actually ~1.33MB on the wire. Restart your web server after changing the config, as these settings don't reload hot.

final_entries.prompt: My SwiftUI view shows the old data even after I update the underlying @State variable — I have to rotate the device to see changes.
final_entries.response: This is likely a binding identity issue — SwiftUI thinks the state hasn't changed because the reference or identity stayed the same. Common causes: (1) You're modifying a mutable property of a struct (e.g., `user.name = "new"`) instead of replacing the whole value (e.g., `user = User(name: "new")`) — SwiftUI detects changes by `Equatable` conformance, and mutating properties don't trigger it. (2) If using `@ObservedObject`, make sure your class publishes the change (`self.objectWillChange.send()` or the property is `@Published`). (3) For collections, SwiftUI uses element identity — if your items don't conform to `Identifiable`, use `id: \self` or `id: \.$id` in your `ForEach`. Quick test: add `.onChange(of: yourState) { print("changed to: \($0)") }` — if it prints but the view doesn't update, the issue is in your view body referencing stale state.
